ch-foundations.html:
Numbers lead to functions

A decimal approximation conveys precision through its last digit. Rounding to \(k\) decimal places has error at most \(\tfrac12 10^{-k}\); truncation gives an interval of width \(10^{-k}\). A certified computation supplies the digits and justifies that error convention.

Start with \(\sqrt2\), then allow any rational \(q\ge0\): the primary object is the function \(q\mapsto\sqrt q\). Likewise \(\pi=4\arctan(1)\) turns a constant computation into a study of arctangent. Rational inputs are the true starting objects. Proved effective continuity supplies irrational evaluations as add-ons.

For every rational \(\varepsilon>0\), construct \(\delta>0\) bounding the change in output for sufficiently close rational inputs. This is the usual \(\varepsilon\)–\(\delta\) definition with an explicit tolerance and evaluation-error budget. It justifies the derived evaluation and independence of the input representation.

The emphasis is on constructions and exact mathematical identities. Quantitative bounds justify them and remain available for numerical corollaries. When a numerical result is requested, specialize a checked computation, choose a sufficient stage from its error bound, and prove the resulting rational inequalities.

Invert the square with two rational lines

The square function is convex. On a positive bracket \([a,b]\), its right-end supporting line \(2bt-b^2\) lies below \(t^2\), and the endpoint secant \((a+b)t-ab\) lies above it. Intersecting them with \(q\) proposes this computation:

\[a'=\frac{q+ab}{a+b},\qquad b'=\frac{b^2+q}{2b}.\]

The formal proof checks rational inequalities directly: \(a\le a'\le b'\le b\), \((a')^2\le q\le(b')^2\), and

\[w'\le\frac{w^2}{2b}\le\frac w2.\]

Starting at \([1,2]\), we compute \(\sqrt2\) with \(w_{n+1}\le w_n^2/2\). Nested intervals, shrinking widths, the quadratic estimate, and agreement with bisection are checked in Lean. Convexity guides the proposal; no formal convexity predicate or general tangent definition is needed by the algorithm.

The computed square root squares to two

Theorem. Let \(s\) be the represented number produced by the preceding computation. Then

\[s\cdot s\simeq 2.\]

Here \(\simeq\) means RealRaw.Equiv, with RealRaw.ofRat 2 on the right. At every stage, the squared lower and upper bounds contain \(2\), so the actual product interval overlaps that exact rational value. The proof uses the construction directly.

ch-integrals.html:
Arctangent motivates integration

The circle-sector computation for arctangent can be expressed by rational rectangles under \(K(t)=1/(1+t^2)\). Refinement bounds the accumulated area for rational endpoints. Replacing this kernel by another specific rational-input function motivates an integral computation.

The integral specification precedes existence. A numerical candidate must earn its integral role through justified cell bounds and shrinking error. Derivatives enter later, when we compare these computations with endpoint formulas.
ch-infinite-series.html:
Arctangent motivates power series

The finite geometric identity for \(1/(1+t^2)\), integrated term by term, produces the arctangent power series and a bounded remainder. A finite prefix plus a tail estimate constructs a rational-input function.

This construction comes before the derivative theory used to compare computations. The next chapter proves concrete secant bounds, FTC, and Taylor estimates. Fourier analysis reuses the finite-prefix and tail method later.
ch-effective-calculus.html:
Construct the derivatives we need

Neighboring secants of the particular square-root and arctangent computations supply bounds. For square root, use \((v-u)/(v^2-u^2)=1/(u+v)\), including the errors in computed roots. For arctangent, finite rectangle comparisons bound each increment by the endpoint kernel values.

Explicit step sizes and evaluation precisions make the secant errors shrink. Finite prefix intersections make the actual derivative intervals nest. The resulting derivatives agree exactly with \(1/(2\sqrt x)\) on positive square-root charts and \(1/(1+x^2)\) on the nonnegative unit arctangent branch.

Its secant is a represented value with its own independent refinement index. A derivative is their common limit for every admissible bracket computation; the bracket family must be inhabited.

ch-rational-circle-trigonometry.html:
Invert arctangent specifically

Solve \(A(u)=\theta/2\) on the selected slope branch \([0,1]\), where \(A\) is geometric arctangent. This is a target-preimage computation. The equation \(\arctan(x)=x\) has only the zero solution and is not the circle construction.

Interval comparisons select a half-bracket. When target and midpoint evaluations overlap, a lower bound on the arctangent increment certifies retaining the central half. Thus every step halves the width, including exact equality cases. The proof checks nesting, shrinking, and the exact target through rational endpoint evaluations.
